claim: Consider a two-age net maternity schedule with strictly positive integer survivorship-weighted reproductive contributions \(a\) at age \(1\) and \(b\) at age \(2\). The exact Euler–Lotka growth factor \(\lambda\) is the positive root of \(\lambda^2=a\lambda+b\), so the exact intrinsic growth rate \(r=\log\lambda\) is strictly increasing in either reproductive contribution. The common generation-time shortcut \(\widetilde r=\log(R_0)/T\), with \(R_0=a+b\) and \(T=(a+2b)/(a+b)\), equals \((a+b)\log(a+b)/(a+2b)\). On the positive-integer grid, adding one unit of late-age reproduction can never decrease \(\widetilde r\) when the initial net reproductive rate satisfies \(R_0\le5\). At initial \(R_0=6\), monotonicity fails for the first time, uniquely at \((a,b)=(5,1)\): adding one age-2 reproductive unit changes the schedule to \((5,2)\), increases the exact growth factor from \((5+\sqrt{29})/2\) to \((5+\sqrt{33})/2\), and increases the exact growth rate from approximately \(1.6472311464\) to \(1.6812526457\), yet decreases the shortcut from \(6\log 6/7\approx1.5357938308\) to \(7\log 7/9\approx1.5134856715\). The shortcut reversal is certified exactly by \(6^{54}>7^{49}\). More generally, with \(S=a+b\), the continuous late-fertility derivative has sign equal to \(2S-a(1+\log S)\), so this is a structural high-early-fertility failure rather than an isolated numerical accident.
integrity: Exact Euler–Lotka monotonicity is proved analytically. The shortcut comparison is reduced to an integer-power inequality and exhaustively checked for every positive schedule through the sharp initial net reproductive rate. The public package includes a replayable standard-library verifier.
scientific_limitations: The sharp boundary concerns two reproductive ages, strictly positive integer survivorship-weighted reproductive contributions, and one-unit additions at the later age. The qualitative derivative mechanism is continuous, but the integer minimality is specific to this discretization.
title: The generation-time growth shortcut first loses fertility monotonicity at net reproduction six
